findings.problem: This is a letter. The true or false statement tests wording the baker hasn't seen yet: the rest of the line in Ephesians 2:2 after "the ruler of the power of the air" ("the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience"). Card 1 gives nothing to reason from, so the baker can only guess. It also brings in "the sons of disobedience" for the first time inside the question.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The quote "But." has a period that isn't in the BSB. Ephesians 2:4 reads "But because of His great love for us..." with no punctuation after "But." Either drop the period from inside the quotation marks or reword so the quote matches exactly.

rule.text: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: In a letter, this blank is the next word of the line in Ephesians 2:4 ("because of His great ___ for us"). The baker can't reason it out from meaning. Card 6 has just said God is "rich in mercy," which fits "pity" as well as it fits "love." So the baker ends up guessing wording they haven't seen.

rule.text: In poetry, letters and prophecy, the rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: This is a where question, but "Outside the gates of heaven" isn't a place from anywhere in the Bible, and "At His feet here on earth" isn't a real Bible location either. The right answer also uses Ephesians' own phrase "heavenly realms," so it sounds more like the Bible than the two wrong answers do.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

findings.problem: Card 12 comes straight after choice card 11 with no story card before it. The new content of Ephesians 2:7 (God's purpose "in the coming ages") first appears inside the question, so no story card sets it up.

rule.text: The setup for a choice is always on a story card.

findings.problem: The stop has 9 story cards and 9 choice cards, which meets the stop rule ("Choice cards are equal to or more than story cards in every stop"). But for letters the docs also say "Fewer choice cards. Tell more of the passage on story cards and save choice cards for the turns that matter." In a letter, a stop can't follow both rules unless the two counts are exactly equal.
findings.question: In poetry, letters and prophecy, which rule wins: choice cards equal to or more than story cards, or fewer choice cards than story cards? Does "fewer" mean fewer than story cards, or only fewer than a narrative passage would have?
